Dave Richeson's Japanese Theorem

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: corners on a circle are joined into triangles, and each triangle has a circle inside it.
How to play: Drag a corner, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Change the number of corners, press Triangulate again, and watch the total.
Look for the math

Move the corners into any order you like and cut the polygon into triangles in a different way: the total shown above stays put. That is the surprise David Richeson proved, extending a temple puzzle from around 1800. The applet itself is Alexander Bogomolny's.

A temple puzzle

The old sangaku took a polygon whose corners lie on a circle and joined one corner to all the others. Add up the radii of the little circles inside those triangles, and the total is the same whichever corner you start from.

Triangles that face backwards

Richeson allowed any triangulation, including polygons with corners out of circular order. Some triangles then wind the other way. Give those a negative radius: a triangle's incircle is drawn blue when its corner order is positive and red when it is negative, and the red radii are subtracted. It is this signed total that never changes.

Why the total cannot change

For a triangle with angles A, B, C on a circumcircle of radius R, its inradius is r = 4R sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2) = R(cos A + cos B + cos C − 1). Each angle is half the arc opposite it. Along an interior cut, the two triangles see complementary arcs, so their cosine terms cancel when the sign of the winding is included. What survives comes only from the polygon's own sides, which is why re-triangulating cannot alter the sum.

What the checks found

The logic test enumerates every sequence of the applet's random cuts for 4 to 9 corners, and checks four different shapes for each: the signed sums agree to a millionth and match R(Σ cos(gap/2) − (n−2)) for convex polygons. It also tries the old fan cuts from every corner up to 12 corners, non-convex orders up to 8 corners, and random layouts right up to the applet's limit of 30. The page's claim holds in all of them. The incircles are rebuilt a second way, straight from the applet's angle-bisector bytecode, and agree with the textbook incenter formula.

Try setting N to 30, dragging one corner across its neighbours, then pressing Triangulate again several times: the number stays the same while the picture changes.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
